title: Incidence-based random walks on simplicial complexes
authors: C. T. Martínez-Martínez, Francisco J. Sevilla
abstract: We introduce an incidence-based random walk on the edges of a random two-dimensional simplicial complex with a complete $1$-skeleton and independently retained triangular faces. The dynamics combine two transport channels, one mediated by vertices and the other by triangular faces, through an effective transition operator controlled by a mixing parameter $q$. This construction isolates the effects of higher-order connectivity without modifying the underlying pairwise support of the walk. We characterize the model through structural observables, spectral relaxation, stationary localization, and first-passage transport. Our results show that partial face retention generates heterogeneous higher-order connectivity, giving rise to a pronounced transport bottleneck at intermediate face densities. In this regime, the second-largest eigenvalue modulus, the inverse participation ratio of the stationary distribution, and the mean first-passage time all exhibit non-monotonic behavior, reaching their largest values at intermediate face densities. The corresponding first-passage-time distributions reveal an enhanced probability of unusually long trajectories. Together, these results establish a simple framework for investigating how heterogeneous higher-order connectivity reshapes spectral and transport properties beyond pairwise network dynamics.
summary: This work develops a framework for random walks on simplicial complexes, modeling transport via two coupled channels: vertex-mediated and face-mediated. By analyzing the effect of partially retained triangles, the authors demonstrate that intermediate levels of structural disorder create a pronounced transport bottleneck. This establishes a simple yet powerful method to quantify how higher-order connectivity reshapes network dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates how incorporating heterogeneous higher-order connectivity (triangles) into a random walk fundamentally alters its spectral and transport properties compared to simple pairwise network dynamics.
main_result: The analysis reveals that the most pronounced transport bottleneck—manifested as maximum mean first-passage time—occurs in an intermediate regime of partial face dilution, suggesting heterogeneity is key.
method: The authors analyze the effective transition operator governing the random walk on the edges of a simplicial complex, using spectral analysis and calculating mean first-passage times.
model_or_system: The model is an incidence-based random walk defined on the edges of a random 2D simplicial complex. The dynamics combine two channels: one mediated by vertices (lower) and one by triangular faces (upper), controlled by a mixing parameter q.
key_observables: Second-largest eigenvalue modulus, inverse participation ratio, mean first-passage time, and the survival probability of first-passage time.
important_parameters: Face retention probability (p) and the mixing parameter (q), which control the degree of higher-order connectivity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the underlying 1-skeleton is fixed (complete graph) and uses a random ensemble approach to study quenched structural heterogeneity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of mean first-passage time on face density (p) and the survival probability of first-passage times across different dilution regimes.
paper_structure: The paper builds the effective transition operator by combining elementary steps via vertices and triangles. It then analyzes the resulting dynamics across different regimes (graph-like vs. fully simplicial) to pinpoint the conditions causing dynamical slowdown.
why_interesting: The study of transport bottlenecks due to structural heterogeneity is highly relevant to understanding energy or information flow in complex, disordered physical systems, which shares conceptual links with glassy dynamics or disordered quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of the two elementary trans- port channels defining the edge walk. Lower transition: the walker moves from an edge (red) to one of its two incident vertices {3, 4}, in the example the walker chose vertex 4, then chooses one edge incident to the chosen vertex, edge (4, 3) in the example. Upper transition: the walker moves from an edge (red) to one of its incident triangles and then to another boundary edge of that triangle.

FIG. 2. Structural properties of the random face-diluted en- semble X(n, p). (a) Mean triangle degree ⟨dT ⟩, (b) standard deviation σ(dT ), and (c) inactive-edge fraction ϕ0, as func- tions of the face-retention probability p. Symbols correspond to different values of n, while the dashed red line indicates the theoretical prediction for n = 16 [Eqs. (24)–(26)].

FIG. 3. Average second-largest eigenvalue modulus ⟨λ∗⟩of the effective transition operator. The top row presents ⟨λ∗⟩ as a function of the face-retention probability p, whereas the bottom row shows the corresponding results as a function of the mean upper degree ⟨dT ⟩= (n −2)p. Columns correspond to q = 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9, respectively. Each symbol represents the average over an ensemble of 180000/n independent real- izations.

FIG. 4. Average inverse participation ratio ⟨IPR(π)⟩of the stationary distribution as a function of the face-retention probability p for a system of size n = 16. Panels (a)–(c) correspond to q = 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9, respectively. The horizontal dashed line denotes the uniform reference value 1/|X1| = 1/120. Error bars represent the standard error over independent realizations.

FIG. 5. Mean first-passage time ⟨MFPT⟩for the effective random walk. (a) Mean first-passage time ⟨MFPT⟩as a function of the face-retention probability p for representative values of the mixing parameter q and fixed system size n = 16. (b) Contour map of ⟨MFPT⟩in the (p, q) parameter space.
